title: A Tax on Sugar?

image.attribution: Romain Behar / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain.

main_content:
The World Health Organization says people around the world are eating more sugar. As a result, it says, health problems related to weight gain and tooth damage are increasing. Sugary foods and drinks cause tooth decay, weakening the bone.

The WHO finds that, on average, the amount of sugar in the foods we eat has risen about 10 percent over the past 10 years. But it has risen at a faster rate in some areas. In the Middle East and North Africa, sugar intake has risen about 15 percent over the past 10 years. In some Asian and Pacific countries, sugar intake is 20 percent higher.

And in South America, people eat more sugar than anywhere else in the world. Francesco Branca is director of the WHO’s Department of Nutrition for Health.

Mr. Branca says reducing how much sugar you eat can be difficult because so many cooks and food-makers add sugar. He says researchers found that 80 percent of the food items in U.S. markets included some kind of sugar.

The WHO is calling on governments to take measures to reduce how much sugar people eat. It proposes taxing products with a lot of sugar and requiring food-makers to list how much sugar can be found in their products.

However, the United Nations agency says it is fine to eat foods that naturally have sugar, such as fresh fruits, vegetables and even milk.

questions.question: What does the World Health Organization say about sugar consumption?
options: Global increase in sugar intake has caused a decrease in health-related issues.
There is a notable rise in health problems related to weight gain and tooth damage due to sugar consumption.
Sugar consumption has remained stable over the last decade across most regions.
The WHO recommends increasing sugar intake to improve overall health.
questions.answer: There is a notable rise in health problems related to weight gain and tooth damage due to sugar consumption.

questions.question: Who is Francesco Branca?
options: An advocate for sugar consumption regulation in the Middle East.
A researcher specializing in Asian food markets.
The director of the World Health Organization’s Department of Nutrition for Health.
A chef known for creating low-sugar recipes.
questions.answer: The director of the World Health Organization’s Department of Nutrition for Health.

questions.question: What makes reducing sugar intake difficult, according to Mr. Branca?
options: The lack of public awareness about sugar sources in food.
The extensive use of sugar by cooks and food manufacturers in many products.
The belief that all sugar consumption is dangerous.
The promotion of low-sugar diets in developing countries.
questions.answer: The extensive use of sugar by cooks and food manufacturers in many products.
